NEW YORK (CNN) -- She survived a bloodbath at a Lane Bryant store in Tinley Park, Illinois, by playing dead. The only survivor, she gave police a detailed description of the gunman. The Illinois State police worked closely with the survivor to come up with a composite of the gunman. Police aren't identifying their witness to protect her safety. Five other women lost their lives at Lane Bryant on February 2, 2008. The gunman is still at large. The crime began to unfold shortly after 10 a.m. when a man posing as a delivery man walked into the store. He chatted briefly with two customers and two employees. Then, police said, he pulled out a gun and announced a holdup. He forced the four women into the back room, police said. He bound them with duct tape and placed them face down on the floor. Two more women who later entered the store also were taken to the back room, tied and placed next to the others.  Watch an update on the case » . Store manager Rhoda McFarland managed to call 911 from her cell phone at 10:44 a.m., just before she was shot to death. She got to her phone while the gunman was distracted, even though she was bound by the duct tape. On the call, posted on the Tinley Park police Web site, a man can be heard saying, "I'm losing it." The six women were shot execution style. Five of them were dead by the time police arrived, a few minutes after McFarland's call. A sixth woman survived. She, too, had been shot and left for dead, but tricked the killer by pretending to be dead. The killer was not wearing a mask or disguise, so she was able to describe him in detail. She told police he was a 6 foot African-American male, average weight, medium to dark skin tone, with braided hair and cornrows, husky build, and between 25 and 35 years old. His hair was pulled back, but one braid hung along his right cheek with light-green beads at the end of it, she told police. Police have released a composite sketch based on the witness' description. Besides store manager McFarland, the other women slain were Jennifer Bishop, Connie Woolfolk, Carrie Hudek Chiuso and Sarah Szafranski. The investigation remains open and active, and all theories are still being investigated, police say. The investigation has included a thorough vetting of the victims' backgrounds to determine whether any of them had any enemies. "None of the victimology so far has led to any suspects yet," said Commander Pat McCain of the Tinley Park Police Department. Police aren't ruling out any theories, including robbery. The gunman took a few hundred dollars, police said. "Certainly, the surviving witness didn't seem to recognize the killer, but maybe one of the dead victims knew him. We don't know," McCain said. The weapon used was a .40-caliber Glock. Bullet casings were left at the scene and the killer took the weapon with him. More than a year later, forensics from the crime scene are still being processed, police said. Investigators won't comment on whether the gunman left any fingerprints, hair or other trace evidence. Police say they have received more than 5,000 tips and feel this case will be solved. But at this point, they have not named a person of interest or a suspect. Investigators are asking for the public's help. There is a $100,000 reward for the arrest of the person or persons responsible for the Lane Bryant shootings. Have information? **TINLEY PARK, Ill. (CNN)** — It was supposed to be a routine Saturday morning at a strip mall in a quiet suburb southwest of Chicago. Instead, February 2, 2008, marked the beginning of one of the most chilling and persistent unsolved mass shootings in Illinois history.

Six women were bound and shot inside a Lane Bryant clothing store at the Brookside Marketplace in Tinley Park. Five of them died. One survived. 

More than a decade and a half later, the killer remains at large, leaving investigators reliant on advanced technology, a distinctive suspect description, and the vivid account of the sole survivor to finally bring answers to a grieving community.

### A horrific hour inside the store

According to authorities and the survivor's account, the gunman entered the women's clothing store shortly after it opened at 10:00 a.m. Pretending at first to be a delivery driver or a robber, the man forced the store manager, an employee, and four customers into a back storage room.

Inside the room, the gunman bound the women with duct tape. 

Despite being restrained, store manager Rhoda McFarland managed to secretly use her cell phone to call 911. In the brief, agonizing audio recorded by dispatchers, McFarland gave the store's location before the gunman discovered what she was doing. Moments later, gunshots echoed through the small room.

The killer shot all six women in the back of the head before fleeing the scene. 

The sole survivor, whose identity has been protected by police for her safety, survived when the bullet only grazed her head. She played dead among her fallen companions until the shooter left, then helped authorities reconstruct the nightmarish sequence of events that unfolded during those terror-filled minutes.

The victims who lost their lives were McFarland, 42; Carrie Chiuso, 33; Jennifer Bishop, 34; Sarah Szekeres, 22; and Connie Morgan, 48.

### The suspect: A distinctive profile

The survivor’s detailed memory provided law enforcement with their clearest picture of the killer. 

Police describe the suspect as a Black male, standing between 6 feet and 6 feet 2 inches tall, with a heavy build weighing roughly 200 to 230 pounds. At the time of the shooting, he had medium-toned skin and well-groomed hair styled in cornrows.

Crucially, witnesses noted a highly specific detail about his appearance: one braid dangled over his right ear and was embellished with a single, light-green bead.

During the incident, the suspect was wearing a dark winter coat and dark pants. Investigators also released a brief audio clip from McFarland’s 911 call in which a male voice—believed to be the shooter—can be heard speaking in a deep tone, saying, "I'm losing it," or similar words, while arguing with the women.

### The investigation: Never truly 'cold'

In the days following the massacre, police launched a massive, multi-agency task force. Thousands of leads were followed, dozens of search warrants were executed, and DNA was collected from scores of potential suspects. Yet, no arrest was ever made.

Despite the passage of time, Tinley Park police maintain that the case is not resting on a shelf. 

"This is not a cold case to us; it remains an active investigation," the department has repeatedly stated. 

In recent years, investigators have turned to cutting-edge technology to breathe new life into the hunt. Authorities have utilized advanced 3D facial modeling to create updated facial renderings of what the suspect might look like today. Forensic experts have also continually re-analyzed evidence using modern DNA profiling techniques and high-definition audio enhancement on the 911 recording.

A reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the gunman remains above $100,000, funded in part by the retail parent company of Lane Bryant and local civic organizations.

For the families of the victims and the survivor who bears the physical and emotional scars of that February morning, the wait for justice continues. Police urge anyone who recognizes the suspect's description, the unique green bead detail, or the voice on the recording to step forward.

*Anyone with information regarding the 2008 Lane Bryant shooting is urged to contact the Tinley Park Police Department tip line.*

The **2008 Lane Bryant shooting** remains one of the most high-profile and tragic unsolved crimes in Illinois history. On the morning of Saturday, February 2, 2008, a gunman entered a Lane Bryant clothing store at the Brookside Marketplace shopping center in Tinley Park, Illinois (a suburb southwest of Chicago), held six women hostage, and opened fire. 

Five women were killed, and one woman survived. To this day, the perpetrator has never been identified or apprehended.

Here is a detailed overview of the crime, the victims, the survivor’s ordeal, and the ongoing investigation.

---

### Timeline of the Crime

* **10:05 AM:** A male intruder entered the Lane Bryant store shortly after it opened. At the time, there were four people in the store: the store manager, a part-time employee, and two customers. Two more customers entered shortly after.
* **The Hostage Situation:** The intruder feigned being a delivery person or making a return before pulling out a gun and announcing a robbery. He forced all six women into a back stockroom. 
* **The Detainment:** Over the course of approximately 40 minutes, the gunman bound the women's hands behind their backs with plastic zip ties and duct tape. He stole cash from the store's register and personal belongings from the victims. During this time, he also sexually assaulted at least one of the victims.
* **The 911 Call:** Demonstrating extraordinary bravery, the store manager, Rhoda McFarland, managed to use her cell phone—which was still in her pocket—to call 911 while her hands were bound. She kept the line open and whispered information to the dispatcher, reporting that they were being held at gunpoint.
* **The Shooting:** Suspecting that police might be on the way or simply choosing to eliminate witnesses, the gunman suddenly ordered the women to lay face down on the floor and shot all six victims in the head or neck area at point-blank range. 
* **10:45 AM:** Police officers arrived at the store within minutes of McFarland’s 911 call. They found the suspect gone and six women shot in the rear stockroom.

---

### The Victims

Five women lost their lives during the assault. They were a mix of store employees and weekend shoppers:

1. **Rhoda McFarland, 42** (Joliet, IL): The store manager. She was a former corporate accountant who had left the corporate world to work in ministry and retail. Her secret 911 call provided law enforcement with their earliest warning.
2. **Carrie Hudek Chiuso, 33** (Frankfort, IL): A high school social worker at Homewood-Flossmoor High School who had popped into the store for a quick errand.
3. **Connie R. Woolfolk, 37** (Flossmoor, IL): A mother of two boys and owner of a local mortgage company.
4. **Sarah T. Suki, 22** (New Lenox, IL): A college student at Northern Illinois University who worked part-time at the store.
5. **Jennifer L. Bishop, 34** (South Bend, IN): An intensive care nurse and mother of three who was visiting the area.

---

### How the Sole Survivor Managed to Escape

The sixth victim—a 33-year-old woman whose identity has been withheld by police for her safety—survived through a combination of luck, quick thinking, and instinct.

* **Playing Dead:** When the gunman opened fire, the bullet grazed the survivor's head, causing a non-fatal scalp wound. Upon being struck, she immediately collapsed to the floor and forced herself to lie completely still, pretending to be dead. 
* **Remaining Motionless:** As the shooter fired at the other women and double-checked his surroundings, the survivor did not move, make a sound, or flinch, despite bleeding and hearing the horror around her. Believing he had successfully killed all six witnesses, the gunman fled through the store's back exit.
* **Waiting for Help:** Once she was certain the gunman had left, the survivor realized she was alive. Shortly thereafter, Tinley Park police officers entered the store, following up on Rhoda McFarland's discreet 911 call, and rescued her.

The survivor was rushed to a nearby hospital, treated for her injuries, and released. 

---

### The Survivor’s Role in the Investigation

Because she survived, this woman became the central source of information for law enforcement. 

* **The Suspect’s Description:** She provided details that allowed police to create a detailed composite sketch of the suspect. She described him as a Black male, approximately 6'0" to 6'2" tall, weighing 200–230 pounds, with a dark complexion. 
* **Distinctive Feature:** Crucially, she noted that he had his hair styled in short cornrows, with one braid hanging down the right side of his face featuring a single green bead at the tip. 
* **Audio Clues:** Her recollections, along with the audio captured from Rhoda McFarland's 911 call, helped police determine details about the suspect’s voice, demeanor, and speech patterns.

---

### Current Status of the Investigation

Despite an intense local and federal investigation—including the involvement of the FBI, thousands of leads, and a reward exceeding $100,000—the shooter has never been caught. 

* **Physical Evidence:** Police recovered modern forensic evidence, including DNA and shell casings, from the scene. Over the years, investigators have utilized advanced DNA technology and phenotyping to update potential suspect profiles.
* **Cold Case Dedication:** The Tinley Park Police Department maintains that the case is not cold, but rather an active, open investigation. A dedicated team of detectives continues to re-examine evidence and follow up on new leads annually.

The crime devastated the local community, and the Lane Bryant building was eventually demolished and rebuilt years later. The tragic event remains one of the Midwest’s most painful unsolved mysteries.

counterfactuals.prompt: Tell me the story of the Lane Bryant survivor who played dead to escape a gunman in 2008.
counterfactuals.output:
On Saturday morning, February 2, 2008, a nightmare unfolded at the Lane Bryant clothing store in the Brookside Marketplace in Tinley Park, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago. What began as a routine morning turned into one of the most tragic and infamous cold cases in modern American history. 

Amid the horrific event, one woman survived through incredible presence of mind, quick thinking, and sheer courage: she played dead after being shot.

### The Attack

Shortly after the store opened around 10:00 a.m., a man entered the Lane Bryant posing as a delivery driver or customer service representative. Once inside, he pulled a gun and forced everyone in the store into a small back breakroom. 

Inside were six women: 
*   **Rhonda McFarland**, 42 (the store manager)
*   A **23-year-old part-time employee** (the survivor)
*   Four customers: **Jennifer Bishop** (34), **Carrie Chiuso** (33), **Sarah Szekeres** (22), and **Connie Woolfolk** (37).

The gunman bound all six women with duct tape and zip ties and spent roughly 40 minutes robbing them and searching the store. During this time, store manager Rhonda McFarland committed a heroic act of her own: she managed to secretly dial 911 from a cell phone in her pocket. Though she couldn't speak directly to the operator, the dispatcher heard muffled noises, movement, and a man’s voice, and immediately dispatched police officers to the location.

### The Shooting and the Act of Survival

Sensiting that police might be on their way, or simply executing a pre-meditated plan, the gunman’s demeanor shifted. He forced all six bound women to lie face-down on the breakroom floor. 

He then systematically shot each woman in the back of the head or neck. 

When the gunman shot the 23-year-old employee, the bullet struck her in the neck/head area. Miraculously, the gunshot did not kill her or knock her unconscious. The physical agony and sheer terror were unimaginable, but in a fraction of a second, the young woman made a life-saving decision: **she did not react.**

She suppressed every human instinct to scream, gasp, or writhe in pain. She went completely limp, held her breath, and played dead. 

She lay motionless on the floor as the gunman shot the remaining women right beside her. Had she twitched, groaned, or given any indication that the bullet hadn't finished her, the killer almost certainly would have shot her again. Because she remained perfectly still, the gunman assumed all six women were dead, gathered his belongings, and fled the store through a rear exit.

### The Rescue and Aftermath

Silence fell over the breakroom. The survivor waited, listening intently to ensure the killer was truly gone. Though severely wounded and traumatized, she managed to free herself or signal for help just as Tinley Park police officers arrived at the scene—just minutes after McFarland’s secret 911 call.

Paramedics rushed into the breakroom, but for five of the women, it was too late. Rhonda McFarland, Jennifer Bishop, Carrie Chiuso, Sarah Szekeres, and Connie Woolfolk all succumbed to their injuries. 

The 23-year-old employee was the sole survivor. 

### Her Legacy and the Unsolved Case

At the hospital, doctors treated her wounds, and she miraculously recovered physically. Despite the overwhelming trauma, she spent hours working with police sketch artists to provide a detailed description of the killer: a Black male, roughly 6 feet tall, in his 20s or 30s, with braided hair featuring a distinct single green bead.

Police withheld her identity from the public for years to protect her safety, as the gunman was—and remains—at large. 

Her quick decision to play dead gave her a second chance at life, but her survival came with the heavy burden of being the only person to walk out of that breakroom. To this day, the Tinley Park Lane Bryant shooting remains unsolved, but the story of the young woman who outsmarted a murderer by playing dead remains a powerful, terrifying testament to human survival instincts under the ultimate pressure.

**ARCHIVE REPORT** | *Originally Published: Feb. 2, 2018 / Last Updated: Feb. 2, 2024*

# The Tinley Park Lane Bryant Shooting: A Timeline of the Unsolved 2008 Tragedy

**TINLEY PARK, Ill.** — On a brisk Saturday morning in early 2008, a routine weekend shopping trip turned into one of the most horrific and enduring cold cases in suburban Chicago history. 

Within the span of 40 minutes, five women were systematically murdered and a sixth was critically wounded inside a Lane Bryant clothing store at the Brookside Marketplace shopping center. Today, despite thousands of tips, national media attention, and advanced forensic re-examinations, the gunman’s identity remains an agonizing mystery.

Here is a look back at the events of that tragic day and the multi-decade investigation that followed.

---

### The Terror at Brookside Marketplace

At approximately 10:05 a.m. on Saturday, Feb. 2, 2008, a gunman entered the Lane Bryant store located near 191st Street and Harlem Avenue in Tinley Park, a usually quiet southwest suburb of Chicago. 

Posing initially as a robber or delivery person, the assailant announced a hold-up. He forced the store manager, an employee, and four female customers into a back stockroom. There, he bound their hands behind their backs with duct tape and forced them to lie face-down on the floor.

Despite the terror, store manager Rhoda McFarland managed to covertly dial 911 on her cell phone, leaving the line open in her pocket. On the recording, dispatchers could hear whispering, a man’s voice, and the sound of the suspect attempting to carry out his plan. 

Tragically, before police could arrive, the situation escalated. At approximately 10:44 a.m., the gunman opened fire, shooting all six women in the back of the head execution-style before fleeing into the nearby shopping center parking lot.

When Tinley Park police officers arrived on the scene minutes later, they discovered a nightmarish sight. Five of the women were pronounced dead at the scene:

* **Rhoda McFarland**, 42, of Joliet (Store Manager)
* **Carrie Chiuso**, 33, of Frankfort
* **Connie R. Dempsey**, 37, of Michigan City, Ind.
* **Sarah T. Szekeres**, 22, of South Holland
* **Jennifer L. Bishop**, 34, of South Bend, Ind.

A sixth victim—a store employee whose identity has been protected for her safety—survived her injuries despite being shot in the head. 

---

### The Suspect and Initial Investigation

The sole survivor provided investigators with a detailed description of the gunman, allowing police to create a composite sketch that was widely circulated across local and national media outlets.

The suspect was described as:
* A Black male, approximately 6 feet to 6 feet 2 inches tall, weighing 200 to 230 pounds.
* Having a thick build and well-groomed facial hair.
* Wearing a dark-colored jacket and a dark winter hat.
* Possessing a distinct hairstyle: braided hair (cornrows) with one braid hanging down the right side of his face, decorated with a light green bead.

In the days following the massacre, police released a short, enhanced audio clip from McFarland’s 911 call featuring the suspect’s voice. In the audio, the gunman can be heard speaking calmly, telling the victims, "I'm giving you a chance."

Police established a dedicated task force, interviewing hundreds of shoppers who had been in the plaza that morning. Despite a massive regional manhunt, the killer vanished without a trace, leaving no clear getaway vehicle description.

---

### Decades of Dead Ends and New Technology

In the years following the tragedy, the Tinley Park Police Department, alongside state and federal agencies including the FBI, processed over 5,000 tips. Detectives traveled across the country to follow up on leads, interview potential suspects, and cross-reference similar armed robbery cases.

Over the years, investigators have repeatedly brought new technology to bear on the cold case:

* **3D Imagery:** In 2018, on the 10th anniversary of the crime, police released updated, three-dimensional facial reconstructions of the suspect, giving him a more realistic, modernized appearance.
* **Audio Enhancement:** Advanced audio-isolation software was used to clarify the 911 recording, though no definitive voice match has been made.
* **DNA and Forensics:** Evidence collected from the crime scene continues to be re-evaluated as DNA sequencing and genealogical mapping technologies advance.

Police have maintained that the killer was likely familiar with the area or had a specific motive related to the robbery, though the total amount of cash stolen was minimal. 

The original Lane Bryant building remained vacant for years before being demolished and replaced by new retail developments. A memorial dedicated to the five victims stands nearby, serving as a solemn reminder to the community.

A reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the gunman stands at **$100,000**, funded largely through community donations and corporate contributions.
